blocks.body:
A Dirichlet character $\chi \bmod q$ is a function on the integers, but it can just as well be read as a function on the ideals $(n)$ of $\mathbb Z$ coprime to $q$. The Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_K(s)=\sum_{\mathfrak a} N\mathfrak a^{-s}$ of a number field $K$ is a sum over ideals of $K$. Hecke asked what the common generalisation should be: which functions $\xi$ on the ideals of a number field give $L$-series $\sum_{\mathfrak a}\xi(\mathfrak a)N\mathfrak a^{-s}$ that still continue to the whole plane and satisfy a functional equation?

His answer, the Größencharaktere (Hecke characters), gives the $L$-functions that control how prime ideals are distributed among ideal classes, ray classes and even angular sectors. They also work in the other direction: some $L$-functions of a field $K$ factor into Dirichlet $L$-functions, so information over $K$ can be carried back to $\mathbb Q$.

blocks.title: From characters of numbers to characters of ideals
blocks.body:
Over $\mathbb Z$ every nonzero ideal is $(n)$ for exactly one $n>0$, so a Dirichlet character $\chi \bmod q$ gives a function $(n)\mapsto\chi(n)$ on ideals coprime to $q$ with nothing to check. In a general ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$ two things change.

1. Not every ideal is principal, so values on non-principal ideals must be chosen consistently with multiplication (this is where class group characters come from).
2. A principal ideal $(\alpha)$ has many generators: $\alpha$ and $\varepsilon\alpha$ for every unit $\varepsilon$. If we want the value $\xi((\alpha))$ to be computed from $\alpha$, the recipe must give the same answer for all generators.

Hecke's idea is to let $\xi((\alpha))$ depend on $\alpha$ in two ways at once: through a congruence condition (the residue of $\alpha$ modulo some ideal $\mathfrak m$, as for Dirichlet characters) and through the position of $\alpha$ in the real and complex embeddings of $K$ (signs at real places, angles at complex places). The unit ambiguity is then absorbed by requiring the product of the two contributions to be $1$ on units.

Write $K_{\mathbb R}=K\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R\cong\mathbb R^{r_1}\times\mathbb C^{r_2}$, where $r_1$ and $r_2$ count real embeddings and pairs of complex embeddings; an element $\alpha\in K$ sits in $K_{\mathbb R}$ through its embeddings.

blocks.title: Hecke character (Größencharakter)
blocks.body:
Let $\mathfrak m$ be a nonzero ideal of $\mathcal O_K$ and $J^{\mathfrak m}$ the group of fractional ideals coprime to $\mathfrak m$. A Hecke character modulo $\mathfrak m$ is a homomorphism $\xi: J^{\mathfrak m}\to\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ for which there exist a character $\xi_f$ of $(\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak m)^\times$ and a continuous homomorphism $\xi_\infty:K_{\mathbb R}^\times\to\{|z|=1\}$ such that
$$\xi((\alpha))=\xi_f(\alpha)\,\xi_\infty(\alpha)\qquad\text{for every }\alpha\in\mathcal O_K\text{ coprime to }\mathfrak m.$$
It has finite order exactly when $\xi_\infty$ depends only on the signs of $\alpha$ at the real places. We extend $\xi$ by $\xi(\mathfrak a)=0$ for integral ideals $\mathfrak a$ not coprime to $\mathfrak m$.

In words: on principal ideals a Hecke character is a Dirichlet-type character of the generator times a continuous "angle" character of the generator, glued so that units see the value $1$.

blocks.title: Three families of examples
blocks.body:
Putting $\alpha=\varepsilon$, a unit, in the definition gives the compatibility condition $\xi_f(\varepsilon)\xi_\infty(\varepsilon)=1$ for all units. Every example below is a way of meeting it.

- Class group characters. Take $\mathfrak m=(1)$ and $\xi_f,\xi_\infty$ trivial. Then $\xi$ is trivial on principal ideals, so it is a character of the class group $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ (see [[class-group]]). More generally the finite-order Hecke characters modulo $\mathfrak m$ are exactly the characters of the ray class group modulo $\mathfrak m$ (with sign conditions at real places allowed).
- Norm characters. $\xi(\mathfrak a)=N\mathfrak a^{i\tau}$ for real $\tau$; here $\xi_\infty(x)=|N(x)|^{i\tau}$. Its $L$-function is just $\zeta_K(s-i\tau)$, a shift.
- Angular characters of $\mathbb Q(i)$. Here $K_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb C$ and the units are $\pm1,\pm i$. For an integer $\ell$ put $\xi_\ell((\alpha))=(\alpha/|\alpha|)^{\ell}$. Replacing $\alpha$ by $i\alpha$ multiplies this by $i^\ell$, so the formula is well defined on ideals exactly when $4\mid\ell$. Since $\mathbb Z[i]$ is a principal ideal domain, this defines $\xi_\ell$ on all ideals. For $\ell\neq0$ it has infinite order: it records the argument of a generator, a continuous quantity.

The third family is the genuinely new one: it sees the argument of $\alpha$ in the complex plane, and Hecke used it to prove that Gaussian primes are equidistributed in angle.

blocks.title: Hecke L-function
blocks.body:
For a Hecke character $\xi$ modulo $\mathfrak m$,
$$L(s,\xi)=\sum_{\mathfrak a}\frac{\xi(\mathfrak a)}{N\mathfrak a^{s}}=\prod_{\mathfrak p\nmid\mathfrak m}\Bigl(1-\frac{\xi(\mathfrak p)}{N\mathfrak p^{s}}\Bigr)^{-1},$$
the sum over nonzero integral ideals and the product over prime ideals. Since $|\xi(\mathfrak a)|\le1$, both converge absolutely for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, by comparison with $\zeta_K(\operatorname{Re}s)$ (see [[dedekind-zeta]]), and the product formula follows from unique factorisation of ideals and multiplicativity of $\xi$ and $N$.

It is the $L$-series of $K$ twisted by $\xi$; for $\xi=1$ and $\mathfrak m=(1)$ it is $\zeta_K(s)$.

blocks.title: Hecke's theorem (finite-order case)
blocks.body:
Let $\xi$ be a primitive Hecke character of finite order of $K$, with conductor $\mathfrak f$ (the smallest modulus from which it comes), and for each real place $v$ let $a_v\in\{0,1\}$ be such that $\xi_\infty(x)=\prod_{v\text{ real}}\operatorname{sgn}(x_v)^{a_v}$. With $\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)$ and $\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s)=2(2\pi)^{-s}\Gamma(s)$, put
$$\Lambda(s,\xi)=\bigl(|d_K|\,N\mathfrak f\bigr)^{s/2}\prod_{v\text{ real}}\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s+a_v)\;\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s)^{r_2}\;L(s,\xi).$$
Then $\Lambda(s,\xi)$ extends to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ satisfying
$$\Lambda(s,\xi)=W(\xi)\,\Lambda(1-s,\bar\xi),\qquad |W(\xi)|=1.$$
It is entire unless $\xi$ is trivial, in which case $L(s,\xi)=\zeta_K(s)$ and the only poles are simple ones at $s=0$ and $s=1$. For Größencharaktere of infinite order the same holds with the gamma factors shifted according to $\xi_\infty$; then $L(s,\xi)$ is entire unless $\xi$ is a norm character $N\mathfrak a^{i\tau}$.

blocks.title: Where the functional equation comes from
blocks.body:
We do not prove Hecke's theorem here; a complete proof takes a chapter (Neukirch, Chapter VII). The idea is the one you have seen for $\zeta(s)$ in [[functional-equation]]. One writes $\Lambda(s,\xi)$ as a Mellin transform (see [[mellin]]) of a theta series: a sum of a Gaussian over the points of an ideal, viewed as a lattice in $K_{\mathbb R}\cong\mathbb R^{n}$, twisted by $\xi$. Poisson summation on that lattice (see [[fourier-poisson]]) relates the theta series at $t$ and $1/t$, and the dual lattice is where $d_K$ and $\mathfrak f$ enter. The root number $W(\xi)$ is a normalised Gauss sum, just as for Dirichlet characters.

Tate's thesis (1950) redid the whole argument as Poisson summation on the adeles, which treats all Hecke characters and all number fields uniformly and is now the standard modern route.

For $\xi$ trivial the formula is the functional equation of $\zeta_K$; for $K=\mathbb Q$ ($d_K=1$, $r_1=1$, $r_2=0$) it is $q^{s/2}\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s+a)L(s,\chi)=W\,q^{(1-s)/2}\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(1-s+a)L(1-s,\bar\chi)$, the functional equation of [[l-functions]], with $a=0$ or $1$ according as $\chi(-1)=1$ or $-1$.

blocks.title: Over the rationals: Dirichlet L-functions
blocks.body:
Take $K=\mathbb Q$ and modulus $(q)$. The continuous characters of $\mathbb R^\times$ are $x\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(x)^a|x|^{i\tau}$ with $a\in\{0,1\}$ and $\tau$ real. So a Hecke character satisfies, for $n>0$ coprime to $q$,
$$\xi((n))=\xi_f(n)\,n^{i\tau},$$
and since $(n)=(-n)$ we also need $\xi_f(-1)(-1)^a=1$. Reading $\xi_f$ as a Dirichlet character $\chi \bmod q$, we get $\xi((n))=\chi(n)n^{i\tau}$ and
$$L(s,\xi)=L(s-i\tau,\chi).$$
Finite order means $\tau=0$, and then $L(s,\xi)$ is literally a Dirichlet $L$-function, with $a$ recording the parity of $\chi$. So over $\mathbb Q$ Hecke's theory recovers Dirichlet's and adds only vertical shifts.

blocks.title: Factorisation over Q(√−3)
blocks.body:
Let $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, with ring of integers $\mathbb Z[\omega]$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, and let $\chi_{-3}$ be the character mod $3$ with $\chi_{-3}(1)=1$, $\chi_{-3}(2)=-1$. For a Dirichlet character $\chi \bmod q$ define $\xi_\chi(\mathfrak a)=\chi(N\mathfrak a)$. Then $\xi_\chi$ is a finite-order Hecke character of $K$ modulo $q\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$
$$L(s,\xi_\chi)=L(s,\chi)\,L(s,\chi\chi_{-3}).$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
For $\alpha\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$ coprime to $q$, the norm $N\alpha=\alpha\bar\alpha$ is a positive integer coprime to $q$, and its residue mod $q$ depends only on $\alpha \bmod q\mathbb Z[\omega]$. So $\xi_f(\alpha)=\chi(N\alpha)$ is a character of $(\mathbb Z[\omega]/q)^\times$, $\xi_\infty=1$ works (norms from an imaginary quadratic field are positive, so units have norm $1$ and $\xi_f(\varepsilon)=\chi(1)=1$), and $\xi_\chi((\alpha))=\chi(N\alpha)$. Multiplicativity of the norm makes $\xi_\chi$ a homomorphism on ideals. Hence $\xi_\chi$ is a Hecke character of finite order.

Now compare Euler factors prime by prime, using how rational primes factor in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ (see [[eisenstein-integers]]):

1. $p\equiv1\pmod3$ splits into two primes of norm $p$. The left side has factor $(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-2}$. On the right, $\chi\chi_{-3}(p)=\chi(p)$, giving the same.
2. $p\equiv2\pmod3$ stays prime, with norm $p^2$. The left factor is $(1-\chi(p)^2p^{-2s})^{-1}=(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}(1+\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}$. On the right $\chi\chi_{-3}(p)=-\chi(p)$: the same.
3. $p=3$ ramifies: $3=-\omega^2(1-\omega)^2$, one prime of norm $3$. Left: $(1-\chi(3)3^{-s})^{-1}$. Right: $(1-\chi(3)3^{-s})^{-1}$ times $1$, since $\chi_{-3}(3)=0$.

If $p\mid q$ all factors involved equal $1$ on both sides. Both sides are absolutely convergent Euler products for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ with equal factors, so they are equal. (With $\chi$ trivial this is the familiar $\zeta_K(s)=\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_{-3})$.)

blocks.title: Why the factorisation matters for zeros
blocks.body:
Both sides continue meromorphically, so the identity holds on all of $\mathbb C$. Suppose that for some $\sigma_0\lt 1$ every finite-order Hecke $L$-function of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ has no zeros in $\operatorname{Re}s>\sigma_0$. Take a Dirichlet character $\chi$ and a point $\rho$ with $\operatorname{Re}\rho>\sigma_0$, $\rho\neq1$. The factor $L(s,\chi\chi_{-3})$ is holomorphic at $\rho$ (its only possible pole is at $s=1$), so $L(\rho,\chi)=0$ would force $L(\rho,\xi_\chi)=0$. At $s=1$ itself the classical non-vanishing $L(1,\chi)\neq0$ for non-principal $\chi$ takes care of the remaining case. So a zero-free half-plane for the Hecke $L$-functions of one quadratic field yields the same half-plane for all Dirichlet $L$-functions. This kind of uniform zero-free half-plane, with $\sigma_0\lt 1$ fixed, is the subject of [[quasi-rh]].

On 30 September 2026 a manuscript produced by an OpenAI internal model claimed that every Dirichlet $L$-function is zero-free in $\operatorname{Re}s>\tfrac78$, using Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, cubic theta sums and a Mellin continuation; it was reported as Lean-verified. This is a claim, not an accepted theorem. The factorisation explains why a statement over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ can bear on Dirichlet $L$-functions; it says nothing about whether the manuscript's argument works.

blocks.title: An angular character on the Gaussian integers
blocks.body: For $K=\mathbb Q(i)$ and $\xi_4((\alpha))=(\alpha/|\alpha|)^4$, compute the coefficients of $2^{-s}$, $5^{-s}$ and $9^{-s}$ in $L(s,\xi_4)$.
blocks.solution:
The coefficient of $n^{-s}$ is $\sum_{N\mathfrak a=n}\xi_4(\mathfrak a)$.

Norm $2$: the only ideal is $(1+i)$. Since $(1+i)^2=2i$, we get $(1+i)^4=-4$ and $|1+i|^4=4$, so $\xi_4((1+i))=-1$. Coefficient $-1$.

Norm $5$: the ideals are $(2+i)$ and $(2-i)$. Now $(2+i)^2=3+4i$ and $(3+4i)^2=-7+24i$, with $|2+i|^4=25$. So $\xi_4((2+i))=(-7+24i)/25$ and $\xi_4((2-i))$ is its conjugate. Coefficient $2\cdot(-7/25)=-14/25$.

Norm $9$: $3$ is inert in $\mathbb Z[i]$, so the only ideal of norm $9$ is $(3)$, and $\xi_4((3))=(3/3)^4=1$. Coefficient $1$.

The coefficients are real, because conjugate ideals have conjugate values, but they are not integers, and they can exceed $1$ in absolute value (at the prime $313$ the coefficient is about $-1.97$). The value $\xi_4((2+i))=(-7+24i)/25$ is not a root of unity, which is another way to see that $\xi_4$ has infinite order.

blocks.title: Checking the factorisation numerically
blocks.body: Let $\chi=\chi_{-4}$, the non-principal character mod $4$. Compute the coefficients of $5^{-s}$, $7^{-s}$ and $25^{-s}$ in $L(s,\xi_\chi)$ for $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ in two ways: directly from ideals, and from the product $L(s,\chi)L(s,\chi\chi_{-3})$.
blocks.solution:
Directly, the coefficient of $n^{-s}$ is $\chi(n)$ times the number of ideals of norm $n$.

- $5\equiv2\pmod3$ is inert, so there is no ideal of norm $5$: coefficient $0$.
- $7\equiv1\pmod3$ splits (for example $7=N(3+\omega)=9-3+1$), so there are two ideals of norm $7$, and $\chi_{-4}(7)=-1$: coefficient $-2$.
- Norm $25$: only the inert prime $(5)$, and $\chi_{-4}(25)=1$: coefficient $1$.

From the product, the coefficient of $n^{-s}$ is $\sum_{de=n}\chi(d)\chi(e)\chi_{-3}(e)=\chi(n)\sum_{e\mid n}\chi_{-3}(e)$.

- $n=5$: $\chi(5)\bigl(1+\chi_{-3}(5)\bigr)=1\cdot(1-1)=0$.
- $n=7$: $\chi(7)\bigl(1+\chi_{-3}(7)\bigr)=-1\cdot2=-2$.
- $n=25$: $\chi(25)\bigl(1+\chi_{-3}(5)+\chi_{-3}(25)\bigr)=1\cdot(1-1+1)=1$.

The two computations agree. In general the number of ideals of norm $n$ in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ is $\sum_{e\mid n}\chi_{-3}(e)$, which is the coefficient form of $\zeta_K=\zeta\cdot L(s,\chi_{-3})$.

blocks.title: Angles of Gaussian primes
blocks.body: Each prime $p\equiv1\pmod4$ is $a^2+b^2$ with $a>b>0$ in exactly one way. Let $\theta_p=\arctan(b/a)\in(0,\pi/4)$. Hecke's angular characters show that the $\theta_p$ are equidistributed in $(0,\pi/4)$. Explain which $L$-functions are involved, and test the statement for $p\lt 2\cdot10^5$ by splitting $(0,\pi/4)$ into four equal parts.
blocks.solution:
The two prime ideals above $p$ are generated by $a+bi$ and $a-bi$, with arguments $\pm\theta_p$. For $4\mid\ell$,
$$\xi_\ell((a+bi))+\xi_\ell((a-bi))=2\cos(\ell\theta_p).$$
Put $\varphi_p=4\theta_p\in(0,\pi)$. The functions $\cos(k\varphi)$, $k\ge0$, are complete for distributions on $[0,\pi]$, so equidistribution of $\varphi_p$ in $(0,\pi)$ (equivalently of $\theta_p$ in $(0,\pi/4)$) follows once
$$\sum_{p\le x,\ p\equiv1(4)}\cos(4k\theta_p)=o\Bigl(\frac{x}{\log x}\Bigr)\qquad(k\ge1).$$
This is a prime number theorem for $\xi_{4k}$. It follows, as for Dirichlet characters, from the continuation of $L(s,\xi_{4k})$ and its non-vanishing on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$. We omit that step.

Numerically, there are $8977$ primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$ with $5\le p\lt 2\cdot10^5$. The counts of $\theta_p$ in the four intervals $[0,\pi/16)$, $[\pi/16,\pi/8)$, $[\pi/8,3\pi/16)$, $[3\pi/16,\pi/4)$ are $2232$, $2241$, $2246$ and $2258$, each within $1\%$ of $8977/4\approx2244$.

blocks.body:
- A Hecke character lives on ideals. A formula in the generator, such as $(\alpha/|\alpha|)^\ell$, defines one only if it is invariant under all units: $4\mid\ell$ for $\mathbb Q(i)$, $6\mid\ell$ for $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$.
- "Größencharakter" is not the same as "finite order". Finite-order Hecke characters are ray class characters and, by class field theory, characters of Galois groups. Infinite-order ones, like the angular characters, are not.
- The clean functional equation is for primitive characters. An imprimitive character differs from the primitive one at finitely many Euler factors, and those factors add zeros on $\operatorname{Re}s=0$.
- A zero-free statement for a product of $L$-functions gives one for each factor, but only away from poles of the other factors. Also, the characters $\chi\circ N$ are a small part of all Hecke characters of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, so a theorem about them alone does not give one about all Hecke $L$-functions of that field.

Dirichlet $L$-functions ([[l-functions]]) are the case $K=\mathbb Q$ and Dedekind zeta functions ([[dedekind-zeta]]) the case $\xi=1$. Their zero-free regions, of the same shape as in [[zero-free-region]] with a possible exceptional real zero as in [[siegel-zeros]], give prime ideal theorems in ray classes and angular sectors. The generalised Riemann hypothesis for them is part of [[grh]]. Cubic residue symbols on $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ (see [[cubic-characters]]), corrected by a character mod $3$ so that they are trivial on the six units, are finite-order Hecke characters of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$. Factorisations such as $L(s,\chi\circ N)=L(s,\chi)L(s,\chi\chi_{-3})$ are how statements over $K$ are brought down to $\mathbb Q$, which is the strategy behind the claimed route to [[quasi-rh]] described above. Values at $s=1$ link to the [[class-number-formula]].

1. Show that $(\alpha/|\alpha|)^\ell$ is well defined on the ideals of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ if and only if $6\mid\ell$.
2. For $K=\mathbb Q(i)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, prove $L(s,\chi\circ N)=L(s,\chi)L(s,\chi\chi_{-4})$ by comparing Euler factors.
3. Explain why, for an imaginary quadratic field, every finite-order Hecke character can be taken with $\xi_\infty=1$.
4. Over $\mathbb Q$, show that a Hecke character modulo $(q)$ of finite order with $\xi_\infty=\operatorname{sgn}^a$ comes from a Dirichlet character $\chi \bmod q$ with $\chi(-1)=(-1)^a$.

sources.ref: Cassels & Fröhlich (eds.), Algebraic Number Theory (contains Tate's thesis)
